summary: Hebrew greetings are few and flexible. שָׁלוֹם (“peace”) says both hello and goodbye; the time of day gives בֹּקֶר טוֹב (answered בֹּקֶר אוֹר), עֶרֶב טוֹב and, when leaving at night, לַיְלָה טוֹב; goodbye is לְהִתְרָאוֹת, “see you” נִתְרָאֶה. There is no formal or informal “you”: Israelis use first names and אַתָּה / אַתְּ with everyone. What changes is gender: מַה שְּׁלוֹמְךָ? to a man, מַה שְּׁלוֹמֵךְ? to a woman — or the casual, gender-free מַה נִּשְׁמַע? Politeness lives in תּוֹדָה, בְּבַקָּשָׁה (please, you’re welcome, here you are) and סְלִיחָה (sorry, excuse me). To introduce yourself say קוֹרְאִים לִי … (everyday) or שְׁמִי … (formal), and answer נָעִים מְאוֹד.

blocks.title: Formality without a polite “you”
blocks.text: Hebrew has no polite pronoun and no polite verb forms: the same אַתָּה / אַתְּ goes to a friend and to a stranger. A formal tone comes from the formula itself (שְׁמִי instead of קוֹרְאִים לִי, עַל לֹא דָּבָר instead of בְּבַקָּשָׁה) and from titles (אֲדוֹנִי “sir”, גְּבִרְתִּי “madam”).

blocks.title: One word, several jobs
blocks.text: שָׁלוֹם = hello and goodbye; בְּבַקָּשָׁה = please, you’re welcome and here you are; סְלִיחָה = sorry, excuse me and pardon? — the situation decides.

blocks.title: Wishes are plain phrases
blocks.text: The greetings are ordinary words, not special verb forms: בֹּקֶר טוֹב is “a good morning”, לַיְלָה טוֹב “a good night”, and לְהִתְרָאוֹת is the infinitive “to see each other”. בֹּקֶר טוֹב — בֹּקֶר אוֹר copies Arabic صَبَاحُ الْخَيْرِ — صَبَاحُ النُّورِ.

blocks.title: Ask yourself before you greet
questions: What time of day is it?
Am I speaking to a man, a woman or a group?

askYourself: Am I arriving or leaving? (Arriving: שָׁלוֹם, בֹּקֶר טוֹב, עֶרֶב טוֹב. Leaving: שָׁלוֹם, לְהִתְרָאוֹת, נִתְרָאֶה, at night לַיְלָה טוֹב.)
What time is it? Morning → בֹּקֶר טוֹב; evening → עֶרֶב טוֹב; going to bed → לַיְלָה טוֹב.
Is the person a man, a woman or a group? → מַה שְּׁלוֹמְךָ / מַה שְּׁלוֹמֵךְ / מַה שְּׁלוֹמְכֶם — or the gender-free מַה נִּשְׁמַע.
Casual or formal? → קוֹרְאִים לִי vs שְׁמִי; בְּבַקָּשָׁה vs עַל לֹא דָּבָר.
Am I asking, thanking or answering thanks? → בְּבַקָּשָׁה / תּוֹדָה / בְּבַקָּשָׁה or עַל לֹא דָּבָר.
Do I need someone’s attention or am I apologizing? → סְלִיחָה.
steps: Ask how they are, in the right gender.
Introduce yourself and answer נָעִים מְאוֹד.

traps: מַה שְּׁלוֹמְךָ is only for a man; to a woman it is מַה שְּׁלוֹמֵךְ.
There is no polite “you” — using אַתָּה / אַתְּ with a stranger or a boss is normal.
לַיְלָה טוֹב is a goodbye, not a greeting when you arrive in the evening (that is עֶרֶב טוֹב).
בֹּקֶר אוֹר only answers בֹּקֶר טוֹב; you never open with it.
עַל לֹא דָּבָר answers thanks; it never means “please”.
קוֹרְאִים לִי does not change for gender; the question is אֵיךְ קוֹרְאִים לְךָ / לָךְ? with “how”, not “what”.

quiz.q: You meet a female friend. How do you ask how she is?
quiz.why: שְׁלוֹמֵךְ with ־ֵךְ is “your” for a woman; שְׁלוֹמְךָ is for a man; בֹּקֶר אוֹר is only the reply to בֹּקֶר טוֹב.

quiz.q: Someone says תּוֹדָה רַבָּה. What do you answer?
quiz.why: בְּבַקָּשָׁה is both “please” and “you’re welcome” (also עַל לֹא דָּבָר).

quiz.q: It is 8 in the morning and a colleague says בֹּקֶר טוֹב. The traditional reply?
quiz.why: “Morning of light”, modelled on Arabic صَبَاحُ النُّورِ. Repeating בֹּקֶר טוֹב is also fine.

quiz.q: You want to pass someone on a crowded bus. What do you say?
How do you address a minister you meet for the first time?
options: with אַתֶּם as a polite plural
with הוּא / הִיא in the third person
quiz.why: Hebrew has no polite “you”; politeness comes from words (בְּבַקָּשָׁה, סְלִיחָה) and titles.

quiz.q: Which greeting does NOT change for gender?
quiz.why: מַה נִּשְׁמַע (“what is heard?”) is the same for everyone; the שְׁלוֹם־ forms carry the gender of “your”.

seeAlso.note: Arabic shares the root of peace: السَّلَامُ عَلَيْكُمْ ~ שָׁלוֹם עֲלֵיכֶם; صَبَاحُ الْخَيْرِ — صَبَاحُ النُّورِ is the model of בֹּקֶר טוֹב — בֹּקֶר אוֹר, and Arabic also changes “you” for a man or a woman.
German chooses du or Sie — a choice Hebrew does not have; bitte matches בְּבַקָּשָׁה in all three uses.
Chinese has a polite 您 beside 你 (您好), and 再见 “again see” matches לְהִתְרָאוֹת; but it splits “please” (请) from “you’re welcome” (不客气).

notes.text: בְּבַקָּשָׁה works like παρακαλώ — please, you’re welcome, here you are. Unlike Greek, Hebrew has no polite εσείς: a stranger is אַתָּה or אַתְּ.

בְּבַקָּשָׁה is used like пожалуйста (please, you’re welcome, here you are) and לְהִתְרָאוֹת like до свидания. There is no ты / вы choice — only the gender of “you” changes: מַה שְּׁלוֹמְךָ / מַה שְּׁלוֹמֵךְ.

There is no tú / usted choice: everyone is אַתָּה / אַתְּ. The time of day works as in Spanish (בֹּקֶר טוֹב ~ buenos días, עֶרֶב טוֹב ~ buenas tardes / noches), but the question “how are you?” changes with the gender of the listener.

English has no gender in greetings; Hebrew asks a man מַה שְּׁלוֹמְךָ? and a woman מַה שְּׁלוֹמֵךְ? — or uses the gender-free מַה נִּשְׁמַע?. One word, בְּבַקָּשָׁה, covers please, you’re welcome and here you are.
There is no tu / vous choice: everyone is אַתָּה / אַתְּ. שָׁלוֹם is both bonjour and au revoir.
בְּבַקָּשָׁה matches bitte in all three uses, and לְהִתְרָאוֹת matches auf Wiedersehen (“to see each other”). The du / Sie choice does not exist: everyone is אַתָּה / אַתְּ.
Hindi नमस्ते is hello and goodbye, like שָׁלוֹם; but Hindi grades respect with आप / तुम / तू, and Hebrew does not — it changes only the gender of “your”: שְׁלוֹמְךָ / שְׁלוֹמֵךְ.
Persian سلام shares its root with שָׁלוֹם (through Arabic), and صبح بخیر is built like בֹּקֶר טוֹב. Persian polite شما has no Hebrew counterpart.

Arabic shares the root of peace (السَّلَامُ عَلَيْكُمْ ~ שָׁלוֹם עֲלֵיכֶם), the reply pattern (صَبَاحُ الْخَيْرِ — صَبَاحُ النُّورِ ~ בֹּקֶר טוֹב — בֹּקֶר אוֹר) and the gendered “you” in كَيْفَ حَالُكَ / حَالُكِ ~ מַה שְּׁלוֹמְךָ / שְׁלוֹמֵךְ.
Turkish selam comes, through Arabic, from the same root as שָׁלוֹם. Turkish also says “good morning / evening / night” by the time of day; but it has the polite siz, which Hebrew lacks.

Japanese greetings change with the level of politeness (おはよう / おはようございます); Hebrew greetings do not — politeness is in תּוֹדָה, בְּבַקָּשָׁה, סְלִיחָה and titles. What changes instead is the gender of the listener.
Korean greetings change with the speech level (안녕 / 안녕하세요); Hebrew has no speech levels — the same שָׁלוֹם and מַה נִּשְׁמַע go to anyone.
Finnish hei / moi are hello, as שָׁלוֹם is; Finnish polite te is rare today, and Hebrew has none at all. Hebrew adds what Finnish lacks: the gender of the listener (מַה שְּׁלוֹמְךָ / שְׁלוֹמֵךְ).
Swahili greetings are a sequence of questions and answers (Habari? — Nzuri!), much like מַה נִּשְׁמַע? — בְּסֵדֶר; but Hebrew changes the question with the listener’s gender, and Swahili does not.
Chinese has a polite 您 beside 你 (您好), which Hebrew lacks. 再见 “again see” matches לְהִתְרָאוֹת, but Chinese splits “please” (请) from “you’re welcome” (不客气), where Hebrew uses בְּבַקָּשָׁה for both.
Vietnamese greetings carry kinship pronouns chosen by age (chào anh, chào chị); Hebrew greetings carry no age or rank — only the listener’s gender, in מַה שְּׁלוֹמְךָ / שְׁלוֹמֵךְ.
Inuktitut asks “how are you?” with a single verb word ending in “you” (Qanuippit?); Hebrew uses a phrase, and the “your” in it changes for a man or a woman (שְׁלוֹמְךָ / שְׁלוֹמֵךְ).
